doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

title: Marx Brothers, Harry Ritz and the longevity of comedy
summary: Admiration for the Marx Brothers, visiting Harry Ritz, and the lost vaudeville circuit that trained comics.

blocks.x: I had an interesting coincidence that I saw a Marx Brothers movie between the time that we had first spoken and I wonder if they were an influence on you?

Yeah I loved the Marx Brothers and the Ritz Brothers. I had the good fortune to meet Harry Ritz before he passed away. He had lived here in Vegas and was in a rest home of sorts. And Joe Delaney who is a newspaper guy, the only real decent critic we’ve ever had here, Joe called me and said, “Harry Ritz is in a home, do you want to go by?” And so went by and spent a couple of afternoons with him and he still was sharp. You know he would forget things but he still was funny.
Well a mutual friend told me to ask you about Chico Marx.

Yeah he was special. He was special. And they were all, I mean Harpo, Chico, they were all incredibly talented. They weren’t just funny, they got it somehow. And I think the criteria for any art form is its longevity. I mean you don’t see people look at the Mona Lisa and say aah, shoulda had more blue, or looking at the Sistine Chapel and say no you should have used more reds. I mean 500 years later you look at that painting and it still takes your breath away. So the real criteria for artists is longevity. And the Marx Brothers are still funny today when you watch them. Abbott and Costello are still funny today. The routines they developed in Burlesque and in Vaudeville, you know, their movies were just an extension of Who’s on First. You know, the two characters created by them in that

one routine. And it took years to create that routine. Unfortunately today that part of the puzzle it no longer exists. Where there used to be theaters where you could work a week at Wilkes Barre, then a week in Philadelphia, a week in Pittsburgh, a week in Allentown, a week in Altoona, then you’d hit Ohio. And then after that there were supper clubs. And that was my background, working supper clubs.
